newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-TWO SCHOOLS OF THOUGHT ON TIGER WOODS'S CHANCES.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TWO SCHOOLS OF THOUGHT ON TIGER WOODS'S CHANCES.

text.p: There are two schools of thought about the chances of Tiger Woods in the British Open which starts on Thursday.
One is that he will win.
The other is that the course will.
When the wind blows at Royal Troon, which it is forecast to do, playing conditions can be testing in the extreme. The back nine in particular, exposed to the sea breezes, have broken many hearts.
Some who have witnessed Woods in his meteoric first year as a professional believe he has the game and the talent to overcome any course in any conditions better than anyone else.
Others, while not denying the brilliance of the 21-year-old American, say lack of experience will be his downfall. And history has many examples supporting them.

A young Jack Nicklaus, brimming with confidence after having just won the U.S. Open at his first attempt as a professional, arrived here in 1962 and hit 80 in the first round. Although he still made the cut, a final-round 79 saw him finish 29 strokes behind the winner, fellow American Arnold Palmer.

Years earlier an even worse fate befell the great Gene Sarazen who was also the U.S. Open champion when he arrived in 1923. At a time when everyone had to play a qualifying round before the competition itself began, Sarazen had to contend with a gale blowing in from the sea and managed only an 85.
He did not even qualify.
Arguably Woods has arrived better prepared than his two illustrious predecessors, armed through videos and advice on the perils of links golf.
He comes not lacking in confidence. "My expectation is to win every tournament. That's my goal, to win every tournament. It's my philosophy, my entire life. I'm not going to change," he said simply.

The doubters say the wind will nullify Woods's prodigious hitting although the youngest U.S. Masters winner in history said he had been working on his swing to lower the trajectory of the flight of the ball.
Precision will be the key over the four days, with fairways exceptionally narrow in places and doglegs leaving players unable to see the green on some of the holes.

"If the wind continues to blow the same way, which I expect it probably will, it is going to take a lot of good, solid shot-making to get round this course the way you want to," said defending champion Tom Lehman. "The fairways out there are so narrow. The rough is up a little bit. I expect the scores won't be real low."

The slightest error can be heavily punished. Double former winner Greg Norman of Australia said: "You're going to have a lot of problems if you're shaping the ball and if you're not hitting the ball the right distance.
"If you don't pitch the right line, you're going to finish in the heather and the gorse. It's very much a precise driving golf course."
South African Ernie Els, winner of last month's U.S. Open and joint second in last year's British Open, said he was anticipating blustery conditions.

"That's the way it should be played. It's wide open, there are no trees, it's really open to all the elements," said Els who missed the cut on his British Open debut as a 19-year-old on this Troon course in 1989.

"I think we're going to find this week a guy winning with a lot of imagination, a guy that can keep his game under control, his shot-making under control. Especially coming in, the fairways are really very narrow, and you've got to take the bad bounces as they come."
The course should hold no surprises for another of the favourites, local-born Colin Montgomerie who has played at Troon since he was 16 and whose father is secretary of the club.
He played down the advantage that would give him. "Once you've played practice rounds, the local knowledge doesn't really mean that much," he said.
"It's only local knowledge (that helps) when it gets a little breezy, and possibly it would favour me if it remains breezy. I've played this course in all types of conditions."
Only one thing is certain. There will be as many people as officials and course conditions permit following young Tiger Woods when he sets out on his opening round on Thursday.
